texts: The shin bone, the main weight-bearing bone of the leg. Its front edge lies just under the skin.
The kneecap, a sesamoid bone inside the quadriceps tendon. It improves the leverage of the thigh muscles.
A toe bone. The big toe has two phalanges and the other toes have three.
One of the five long bones of the foot, between the tarsal bones and the toes.
The ankle bone that sits between the leg bones and the heel, transmitting body weight to the foot.
The heel bone, the largest bone of the foot. The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon attaches to it.
The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. It runs from the hip joint to the knee.
The slender outer bone of the leg. It carries little weight but anchors muscles and forms the outer ankle.
Formed by the fused ilium, ischium and pubis. The two hip bones and the sacrum form the pelvis.
A permanent tooth. Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars grind food.
A triangular bone formed by five fused vertebrae. It joins the hip bones at the sacro-iliac joints.
A cervical vertebra of the neck. Cervical vertebrae have small bodies and openings in their transverse processes for the vertebral arteries.
The second cervical vertebra. Its dens acts as the pivot on which the atlas and skull rotate.
The first cervical vertebra. It supports the skull and allows nodding at the atlanto-occipital joint.
A lumbar vertebra. The five lumbar vertebrae have the largest bodies, carrying most of the upper body's weight.
A thoracic vertebra. Each of the twelve thoracic vertebrae articulates with a pair of ribs.
The tailbone: three to five small fused vertebrae at the base of the spine.
A U-shaped bone in the neck that does not touch any other bone. It anchors the tongue and muscles used in swallowing.
The lower jaw, the only movable bone of the skull. It holds the lower teeth and moves at the temporomandibular joint.
The anvil, the middle ear ossicle that passes vibration from the malleus to the stapes.
The stirrup, the smallest bone in the body. It presses on the oval window of the inner ear.
The hammer, the outermost of the three middle-ear ossicles. It is attached to the eardrum.
One of a pair of curved plates forming the top and sides of the cranial vault.
One of two small bones forming the bridge of the nose.
Forms the side and base of the skull. It houses the middle and inner ear and joins the mandible at the jaw joint.
A light, spongy bone between the orbits that forms part of the nasal cavity and its walls.
The upper jaw bone. It holds the upper teeth and forms part of the orbit, nose and hard palate.
The cheekbone. It forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the orbit.
Forms the back and base of the skull. The spinal cord passes through its foramen magnum.
Forms the forehead and the roofs of the orbits. It contains the frontal sinuses.
A butterfly-shaped bone at the centre of the skull base. It holds the pituitary gland in the sella turcica.
One of a pair of small cartilages that move the vocal cords.
The largest cartilage of the larynx. It forms the Adam's apple.
A ring-shaped cartilage at the base of the larynx, the only complete cartilage ring in the airway.
Hyaline cartilage joining a rib to the sternum or to the cartilage above. It lets the chest wall flex during breathing.
A true rib: it attaches to the sternum through its own costal cartilage.
A false rib: its costal cartilage joins the cartilage of the rib above rather than the sternum.
A floating rib: short and with no anterior attachment.
The upper part of the breastbone. It joins the clavicles and the first pair of ribs.
The long middle part of the breastbone, to which the second to seventh costal cartilages attach.
The small lower tip of the sternum. It is cartilage in youth and slowly ossifies with age.
The forearm bone on the little-finger side. It forms the main hinge of the elbow.
A finger bone. Each finger has three phalanges and the thumb has two.
One of the five long bones of the palm, between the wrist and the fingers.
One of the eight carpal bones of the wrist, arranged in two rows.
The bone of the upper arm, from the shoulder joint to the elbow.
The forearm bone on the thumb side. It rotates around the ulna to turn the palm up or down.
The shoulder blade. Its glenoid cavity forms the shoulder joint with the humerus, and many shoulder muscles attach to it.
The collarbone. It braces the shoulder away from the chest and is the only bony link between the arm and the trunk.
A nearly circular fibrocartilage pad cushioning the outer side of the knee joint.
A knee ligament that stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur. It is often torn in sports.
A C-shaped fibrocartilage pad cushioning the inner side of the knee joint.
A knee ligament that stops the tibia sliding backward on the femur.
A band inside the vertebral canal along the back of the vertebral bodies. It limits forward bending.
A strong band along the front of the vertebral bodies that limits backward bending of the spine.
Elastic ligaments joining the laminae of neighbouring vertebrae; their yellow colour comes from elastin.
A fibrocartilage pad between two vertebral bodies that absorbs shock and allows the spine to bend.
A hip muscle that keeps the pelvis level when standing on one leg.
A thick band of fascia along the outer thigh, from the hip to below the knee. It steadies the knee and hip.
The largest muscle of the body. It extends the hip, as when climbing stairs or standing up.
The smallest and deepest gluteal muscle. It helps gluteus medius stabilise the pelvis.
The muscle at the front of the shin that lifts the foot (dorsiflexion).
An inner-thigh muscle that pulls the leg toward the midline.
A long thin muscle of the inner thigh that adducts the hip and flexes the knee.
The largest adductor muscle of the inner thigh. It pulls the leg inward and helps extend the hip.
A muscle on the outer leg that turns the sole outward and supports the arch of the foot.
The head of the biceps femoris that crosses only the knee, which it bends.
A hamstring muscle on the back of the thigh that bends the knee and extends the hip.
A hamstring muscle on the back and inner thigh that bends the knee and extends the hip.
The outer hamstring head that crosses the hip and knee. It bends the knee and extends the hip.
Outer head of the calf muscle. Gastrocnemius points the foot and helps bend the knee.
A broad calf muscle under the gastrocnemius. It points the foot and is key for standing and walking.
Inner head of the calf muscle. Gastrocnemius points the foot and helps bend the knee.
The Achilles tendon, the thickest tendon in the body. It joins the calf muscles to the heel bone.
A deep hip muscle that rotates the thigh outward. The sciatic nerve usually passes just below it.
The inner quadriceps muscle. It extends the knee and helps keep the kneecap on track.
The largest quadriceps muscle, on the outer thigh. It extends the knee.
The longest muscle in the body, running diagonally across the thigh. It flexes hip and knee, as when sitting cross-legged.
The quadriceps muscle that crosses both hip and knee. It flexes the hip and extends the knee.
The deep quadriceps muscle under rectus femoris. It extends the knee.
A long muscle from the lumbar spine to the femur. With iliacus it is the main hip flexor.
Lines the inside of the pelvis and joins psoas major to flex the hip.
The forehead muscle that raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead.
The outer ring of the muscle around the eye, used to squeeze the eyelids tightly shut.
The part of the eyelid muscle that closes the eyelids gently, as in blinking.
A facial muscle that draws the corner of the mouth up and out when smiling.
The ring muscle around the lips. It closes and purses the mouth.
A fan-shaped chewing muscle on the side of the head that closes the jaw.
Part of the masseter, the strongest chewing muscle, which raises the mandible to clench the jaw.
Deeper part of the masseter, the strongest chewing muscle, which raises the mandible.
A broad back muscle that pulls the arm down and back, as in climbing or rowing.
Middle fibres of the trapezius. They pull the shoulder blades together.
Lower fibres of the trapezius. They depress the shoulder blade and help rotate it upward.
Upper fibres of the trapezius. They elevate the shoulder blade, as in shrugging.
A muscle between the spine and the shoulder blade that retracts and stabilises the scapula.
Lies under the biceps and is the main flexor of the elbow.
One of the two heads of the biceps. It bends the elbow and turns the palm up.
A forearm muscle that bends the elbow, strongest with the forearm half-turned.
A rotator cuff muscle above the spine of the scapula. It starts raising the arm and steadies the shoulder joint.
The largest rotator cuff muscle, on the front of the scapula. It rotates the arm inward.
A small rotator cuff muscle that rotates the arm outward.
A rotator cuff muscle below the spine of the scapula that rotates the arm outward.
The front part of the deltoid. It raises the arm forward and rotates it inward.
The back part of the deltoid. It draws the arm backward and rotates it outward.
The middle part of the deltoid, which raises the arm out to the side.
A muscle from the scapula to the humerus that draws the arm down, back and inward.
The deep head of the triceps, the muscle that straightens the elbow.
The outer head of the triceps, the muscle that straightens the elbow.
The head of the triceps that crosses the shoulder. The triceps straightens the elbow.
The deep fascia enclosing the thigh muscles like a stocking.
The dome-shaped main muscle of breathing, separating the chest from the abdomen. It flattens to draw air into the lungs.
A thin muscle under pectoralis major that pulls the shoulder blade forward and down.
Muscles between the ribs that lift the rib cage during breathing in.
A saw-toothed muscle on the side of the chest that holds the shoulder blade against the ribs and rotates it upward.
Upper part of the main chest muscle. It flexes the arm forward and up.
The large lower part of the main chest muscle. It pulls the arm down and across the chest.
The lowest fibres of pectoralis major, arising from the sheath of the rectus abdominis.
Muscles between the ribs that help pull the rib cage down during forced breathing out.
A neck muscle running from the sternum and clavicle to behind the ear. It turns and flexes the head.
A thin sheet of muscle in the skin of the neck that tenses the neck skin and pulls down the corners of the mouth.
The outermost flat muscle of the side of the abdomen. It twists and flexes the trunk and compresses the abdomen.
The middle layer of the abdominal wall, under the external oblique. It works with it to rotate the trunk.
A fibrous line down the middle of the abdomen where the abdominal wall aponeuroses meet.
The paired vertical muscle at the front of the abdomen (the 'six-pack'). It flexes the trunk.
The deepest abdominal wall muscle. Its fibres run horizontally and act like a corset to compress the abdomen.
A fold of dura mater that roofs over the cerebellum and separates it from the cerebrum.
A sickle-shaped fold of dura mater between the two cerebral hemispheres.
The tough outer membrane enclosing the spinal cord and its nerve roots.
The nerve fibre tracts beneath the cerebral cortex that connect brain regions.
The broad band of nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
One of a pair of fluid-filled cavities in the cerebral hemispheres that make cerebrospinal fluid.
A narrow fluid-filled cavity between the two halves of the thalamus.
A relay centre deep in the brain that passes sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex.
A small region below the thalamus that controls hunger, thirst, body temperature and the pituitary gland.
The lowest part of the brainstem. It controls heart rate, breathing and blood pressure.
The top part of the brainstem, involved in eye movement, hearing and visual reflexes.
A fluid-filled cavity between the brainstem and the cerebellum.
The part of the brainstem that relays signals to the cerebellum and helps control breathing.
Nerve fibre tracts around the spinal grey matter that carry signals up to and down from the brain.
Grey matter of the spinal cord that receives sensory input from the body.
Grey matter of the spinal cord containing the motor neurons that drive skeletal muscles.
A chain of ganglia beside the spine carrying the 'fight or flight' nerves of the autonomic system.
Cranial nerve III. It moves most eye muscles, raises the eyelid and narrows the pupil.
Cranial nerve I, carrying the sense of smell from the nose to the brain.
Cranial nerve XII, which moves the tongue.
Cranial nerve V, the main sensory nerve of the face and the motor nerve for chewing.
Cranial nerve II, carrying visual information from the retina to the brain.
Cranial nerve IX, serving taste and sensation at the back of the tongue and the pharynx.
Cranial nerve X, the longest cranial nerve. It supplies the heart, lungs and most of the gut and slows the heart rate.
Cranial nerve VII. It controls the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue.
Cranial nerve VIII, carrying hearing and balance from the inner ear.
Supplies the muscles that straighten the elbow, wrist and fingers.
Winds around the neck of the humerus to supply the deltoid and teres minor.
Supplies most forearm flexors and the thumb muscles. It is the nerve compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Supplies most small muscles of the hand. It is the 'funny bone' nerve at the elbow.
Part of the brachial plexus, the network of nerves from C5–T1 that supplies the shoulder, arm and hand.
Supplies the biceps and brachialis, then the skin of the outer forearm.
Supplies the quadriceps and the skin of the front of the thigh.
A branch of the femoral nerve supplying the skin of the inner leg and foot.
The thickest nerve in the body, running from the lower spine through the buttock to the back of the thigh.
A branch of the sciatic nerve supplying the calf muscles and the sole of the foot.
A branch of the sciatic nerve that winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is easily injured.
Cranial nerve XI, which moves the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
The nerves running between the ribs, supplying the intercostal muscles and the skin of the chest and abdomen.
The bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord, named for its resemblance to a horse's tail.
The clear front window of the eye that does most of the focusing of light.
The coloured ring of the eye. Its muscles widen or narrow the pupil.
A clear, flexible structure behind the iris that fine-tunes focus for near and far vision.
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that converts light into nerve signals.
The tough white outer coat of the eyeball.
The eardrum, which vibrates with sound and passes it to the ossicles.
The snail-shaped part of the inner ear that converts sound into nerve signals.
Carries blood to the arm and gives branches to the neck, brain and chest wall.
The continuation of the subclavian artery through the armpit.
The main artery of the upper arm, felt on the inner elbow when measuring blood pressure.
A forearm artery on the thumb side, where the pulse is usually taken at the wrist.
A forearm artery on the little-finger side that supplies the hand through the palmar arches.
The main artery of the thigh. Its pulse can be felt in the groin.
The largest branch of the femoral artery, supplying the muscles of the thigh.
The continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee.
The main artery of the neck. It divides into the internal carotid (brain) and external carotid (face and scalp).
The first branch of the aortic arch. It divides into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.
The aorta below the diaphragm. It supplies the abdominal organs and divides into the common iliac arteries.
Carries blood from the aorta to a kidney. The kidneys receive about a fifth of the heart's output.
Supplies the small intestine and the first half of the large intestine.
One of the two terminal branches of the aorta. It divides into the internal and external iliac arteries.
Supplies the leg. It becomes the femoral artery as it passes under the inguinal ligament.
The first part of the aorta, rising from the left ventricle. The coronary arteries branch from it.
The part of the aorta that descends through the chest, giving branches to the chest wall, oesophagus and bronchi.
The vessel leaving the right ventricle that divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries to the lungs.
A small muscle in a ventricle that anchors the valve leaflets through tendinous cords, so they do not invert.
A cusp of the pulmonary valve, which stops blood flowing back from the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle.
A leaflet of the tricuspid valve, which stops blood flowing back from the right ventricle into the right atrium.
A cusp of the aortic valve, which stops blood flowing back from the aorta into the left ventricle.
A wide vein in the groove at the back of the heart that drains the cardiac veins into the right atrium.
A superficial neck vein draining the scalp and face. It is often visible under the skin.
A superficial arm vein along the little-finger side, often used for blood samples near the elbow.
A superficial arm vein along the thumb side that drains into the axillary vein.
The large vein returning blood from the head, neck and arms to the right atrium.
Carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach, intestines, pancreas and spleen to the liver.
The main vein draining the brain, face and neck. It runs beside the carotid artery.
A superficial vein running up the back of the calf to the back of the knee.
The longest vein in the body, running under the skin from the inner foot to the groin. It is often used for bypass grafts.
The short final segment of the inferior vena cava, entering the right atrium just above the diaphragm.
The largest vein. It returns blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen to the heart.
The double membrane lining the chest cavity and covering the lungs. Fluid between its layers lets the lungs glide.
The largest internal organ. It processes nutrients, makes bile and proteins, stores energy and breaks down toxins.
A small sac under the liver that stores and concentrates bile.
A gland behind the stomach that makes digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.
The muscular back part of the roof of the mouth. It rises to close off the nose when swallowing.
The largest salivary gland, in front of the ear.
A salivary gland under the jaw that makes most of the saliva at rest.
The smallest of the major salivary glands, under the tongue.
A muscular organ for tasting, chewing, swallowing and speech.
The middle part of the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed.
The first part of the small intestine, where bile and pancreatic juices mix with food.
A muscular J-shaped sac that churns food with acid and enzymes to begin digesting proteins.
The part of the large intestine rising on the right side of the abdomen.
The S-shaped final part of the colon that leads to the rectum.
The part of the large intestine descending on the left side of the abdomen.
The part of the large intestine crossing the upper abdomen.
A narrow, finger-like pouch from the caecum containing lymphoid tissue.
The muscular tube carrying food from the pharynx to the stomach.
A fold of peritoneum between the liver and the stomach.
An apron-like fold of peritoneum hanging from the stomach over the intestines. It stores fat and helps limit infection.
The funnel inside the kidney that collects urine and leads into the ureter.
A bean-shaped organ that filters blood to make urine and helps control blood pressure.
A muscular tube carrying urine from the kidney to the bladder.
The tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body; in males it also carries semen.
A muscular sac in the pelvis that stores urine.
One of usually four tiny glands behind the thyroid that control blood calcium.
A butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that makes hormones controlling metabolism.
The adrenal gland on top of the kidney. It makes cortisol, aldosterone and adrenaline.
A small gland in the brain that makes melatonin, helping regulate sleep.
The back lobe of the pituitary, which releases oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone made in the hypothalamus.
The front lobe of the pituitary gland, which makes hormones controlling growth, the thyroid, the adrenals and reproduction.
Erectile tissue surrounding the urethra, expanding at the end to form the glans.
One of two columns of erectile tissue along the top of the penis.
The sensitive tip of the penis, formed by the corpus spongiosum.
The tube that carries sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct.
The male gonad, which produces sperm and testosterone.
A coiled tube on the back of the testis where sperm mature and are stored.
A gland behind the bladder that contributes most of the fluid in semen.
A gland below the bladder surrounding the urethra. It adds fluid to semen.
A leaf-shaped flap that folds over the entrance to the larynx during swallowing.
A lobar bronchus, supplying one lobe of the lung.
A segmental bronchus, supplying one bronchopulmonary segment, the smallest surgically removable unit of the lung.
The windpipe, a tube held open by C-shaped cartilage rings, leading from the larynx to the bronchi.
The lower lobe of the left lung, resting on the diaphragm.
The upper lobe of the left lung, including the lingula that lies against the heart.
The lower lobe of the right lung, resting on the diaphragm.
The upper lobe of the right lung.
The middle lobe, found only in the right lung.
A group of lymph nodes, small filters along lymphatic vessels where immune cells meet foreign material.
An organ in the upper left abdomen that filters the blood, removes old red cells and helps fight infection.
Subcutaneous fat (hypodermis): insulation and an energy store between the skin and the muscles. Modelled approximately in this app.
